t: Most archaeologists consider the Erlitou culture, centred on a palace city in Henan, the first state-level society in China.
Erlitou was the earliest large-scale bronze-producing culture in China, and the city monopolised the casting of ritual bronze vessels, among them the earliest ding.
Chinese archaeologists generally identify it with the later part of the Xia dynasty, but some Western scholars call this premature, since no contemporary writing has been found to prove the link.
dyk: Tracks of vehicles found near the palace area at Erlitou are the earliest evidence of wheeled wagons in China.
ev: An outburst flood at Jishi Gorge destroys the Lajia site on the upper Yellow River, a flood some authors link to the later Xia flood myth
By radiocarbon dating the Erlitou culture begins, and Erlitou grows quickly into a regional centre of several thousand people
A walled city is built at Yanshi, 6 km northeast of Erlitou, which the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project takes as the founding of the Shang
In the Upper Erligang phase all the palaces of Erlitou are abandoned and the city shrinks to a village of 30 ha
Xu Xusheng discovers the Erlitou site and suggests it was Bo, the first capital of the Shang
Archaeologists in China begin to identify Erlitou with Zhenxun, the last capital of the Xia
Radiocarbon studies narrow the culture’s dates to 1750–1500 BCE
The Erlitou Site Museum of the Xia Capital, with more than 2,000 objects from the site, opens in Luoyang

f.homeland: The Yellow River valley: Henan and Shanxi, later also Shaanxi and Hubei; the type site at Erlitou in Yanshi, Henan, on the Yi River, a tributary of the Luo.
f.period: Early estimates c. 1900–1500 BCE; radiocarbon dating since 2007 gives 1750–1500 BCE. The Erlitou site grew in four phases; Phase IV overlaps the Lower Erligang culture (1600–1450 BCE), and in the Upper Erligang phase (1450–1300 BCE) Erlitou shrank to a village.
f.known: the palace city of Erlitou, with its walled palace complex and courtyards; the earliest large-scale bronze casting in China, in section moulds; the earliest bronze ding and the first bronze dagger-axes; early metal bells; jade ritual blades (zhang) and dagger-axes (ge); the earliest tracks of wheeled vehicles in China; symbols on pottery
f.sources: Excavations at Erlitou, discovered in 1959 by Xu Xusheng; radiocarbon dating since 2007; the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project; traditional accounts written down much later, such as the Bamboo Annals and the Records of the Grand Historian. No contemporary written records have been found.
